bibl.title: The Effects of Cognitive and Noncognitive Abilities on Labor Market Outcomes and Social Behavior

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: This paper established that a low dimensional vector of cognitive and noncognitive skills explains a variety of labor market and behavioral outcomes.

span.label: cognitive and noncognitive skills as determinants of labour-market and behavioural outcomes
span.quote: This paper presents an analysis of the effects of both cognitive and noncognitive skills on wages, schooling, work experience, occupational choice and participation in a range of adolescent risky behaviors.

span.label: latent-factor-econometric-modelling
span.quote: Our model is a factor model with endogenous factor loadings.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A single low-dimensional pair of latent abilities acts as the common cause generating the observed clustering of risky adolescent behaviors together with schooling and wage outcomes.
span.quote: Our analysis explains the phenomenon of correlated risky behaviors using the same low dimensional model of latent skills that explains wages, employment and schooling attainment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Noncognitive skills raise wages along two routes: directly by raising productivity, and indirectly by raising schooling attainment and accumulated work experience.
span.quote: and family background effects, raise wages through their direct effects on productivity as well

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The GED wage penalty arises because GED holders' deficit in noncognitive skill lowers employment and work-experience accumulation and removes a trait the market pays for.
span.quote: have lower noncognitive skills than dropouts (see Figure 3) and hence are less likely to be employed

span.label: The paper does not estimate the separate channels (preferences, discount rate, human-capital productivity, market productivity) through which the abilities operate.
span.note: what this limits: any mechanistic reading of the results: WE DO NOT ESTIMATE RELATIONSHIPS FOR EACH OF THE CHANNELS THROUGH WHICH COGNITIVE AND NONCOGNITIVE ABILITIES MIGHT OPERATE
span.quote: In this paper, we do not estimate relationships for each of the channels through which cognitive and noncognitive abilities might operate.

span.label: Collapsing noncognitive skill into a single latent factor is unlikely to capture all its aspects.
span.note: what this limits: every claim stated in terms of noncognitive skill: THERE ARE MANY ASPECTS ... SELF CONTROL, TIME PREFERENCE, SOCIABILITY ... IT IS LESS LIKELY THAT ONE TRAIT CAPTURES ALL ASPECTS - the construct is collapsed to one latent factor
span.quote: Since there are many aspects of noncognitive skills – self control, time preference, sociability, and so forth – it is less likely that one trait captures all aspects of these behaviors.

span.label: Support conditions for semiparametric identification are not met, so results rest on the parametric structure of the model.
span.note: what this limits: every estimate in the paper: THE EMPIRICAL RESULTS THAT WE GENERATE ARE IDENTIFIED FROM THE PARAMETRIC STRUCTURE OF THE MODEL - the support conditions for semiparametric identification are not met, so the answers come from the assumed form
span.quote: This evidence suggests that the empirical results that we generate are identified from the parametric structure of the model.

span.label: The underlying theoretical model is static and ignores the timing of decisions.
span.note: what this limits: any conclusion about sequencing or timing: OUR THEORETICAL MODEL IS STATIC AND DOES NOT CONSIDER THE TIMING OF DECISIONS
span.quote: Our theoretical model is static and does not consider the timing of decisions.

span.label: The corroborating CNLSY79 data lack adult outcomes and have small samples.
span.note: what this limits: the CNLSY79 corroboration only: MANY OF THE CHILDREN ARE STILL YOUNG AND WE LACK INFORMATION ON THEIR WAGES, OCCUPATIONAL STATUS AND EMPLOYMENT AT AGE 30
span.quote: A disadvantage of these data is that many of the children are still young and we lack information on their wages, occupational status and employment at age 30.

span.label: The noncognitive measures used (Rotter, Rosenberg) are narrower than would be ideal and are not linked to economic preference parameters.
span.note: what this limits: the interpretation of the noncognitive measures: IT WOULD BE BETTER TO USE A WIDER ARRAY OF PSYCHOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS AND ... TO CONNECT THEM WITH MORE CONVENTIONAL MEASURES OF PREFERENCE PARAMETERS IN ECON[omics]
span.quote: Ideally, it would be better to use a wider array of psychological measurements and, as previously noted, to connect them with more conventional measures of preference parameters in economics.

span.label: The scale of the two latent abilities is not measured but set: two normalizations are stated to be required for identification, and they fix the scale of the factors.
span.note: what this limits: the magnitude of a factor score as a quantity of ability: the paper states two normalizations are required for identification and that they set the scale of the factors
span.quote: As explained in Section (3.5) two normalizations are required to assure identification of the model. These set the scale of the factors.

span.label: The direction of the bias in the conventional estimates is stated to be unknown, because the problems push in different directions.
span.note: what this limits: treating an OLS estimate as a bound on the effect: the paper states the biases run in different directions so the sign of the difference from its own model cannot be predicted
span.quote: Because these problems likely bias the estimates in different directions, we cannot predict whether OLS estimates will be higher or lower than those of our model.

span.label: The measures used are declared imperfect: the attitude scales proxying noncognitive ability are affected by family background and are called at best imperfect measures of true ability.
span.note: what this limits: any test score read as the ability itself: the paper states these scores are affected by family background and are at best imperfect measures of an individual's true abilities
span.quote: In addition, scores on the attitude scales used to proxy noncognitive ability, as well as the cognitive scores, are likely to be affected by family background characteristics, and are at best imperfect measures of an individual’s true noncognitive and cognitive abilities.

span.label: What the construct covers is bounded by the instrument available in the survey, and the authors say a wider array of psychological measurement would have been better.
span.note: what this limits: the noncognitive factor as the full space of noncognitive ability: the authors state a wider array of psychological measurements would ideally have been used
span.quote: Ideally, it would be better to use a wider array of psychological measurements and, as previously noted, to connect them with more conventional measures of preference parameters in economics.

span.label: The channels through which the abilities act are not separately estimated; the model is a linear-in-the-parameters approximation.
span.note: what this limits: attributing an effect to a particular channel: the paper states it does not estimate the relationships for each channel separately and that its model approximates the general one
span.quote: Our econometric model is a linear-in-the-parameters approximation to this general model. In this paper, we do not estimate relationships for each of the channels through which cognitive and noncognitive abilities might operate.

span.label: An interchangeability the paper asserts in principle is explicitly deferred rather than shown.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that test scores and behaviours are interchangeable proxies: the paper states this in principle and leaves the task for future work
span.quote: In principle, one can determine which factors are common across tests and preference parameters. Test scores and behaviors can be used interchangeably to proxy factors. This task is left for future work.

span.label: The disputed word in this literature is 'importance', and the paper's claim holds under one sense of it and reverses under another that the paper states in the same sentence: cognitive skills explain much more of the variance of log wages, while the skill gradients of the two abilities are similar. The paper marks its choice ('for the sense of importance adopted in this paper') rather than leaving it implied, which is what makes the reversal checkable at all.
span.quote: For many dimensions of behavior and for the sense of “importance” adopted in this paper, noncognitive ability is as important, if not more important, than cognitive ability.

span.label: The authors take the latent-variable measurement models built in psychometrics and extend them so that a choice variable (schooling) and background variables can enter the measurement equations of an economic model.
span.quote: the problems of endogeneity and measurement error. Our method extends the LISREL model

span.label: two psychology instruments - the Rotter Locus of Control Scale and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale - are imported into labour economics to stand for noncognitive skill
span.quote: The noncognitive measures available in the data set are the Rotter Locus of Control Scale which was administered in 1979 and the Rosenberg 5 Self-Esteem Scale which was administered in 1980.

span.label: cognitive skill is measured with five subtests of the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery, an instrument built for military selection and re-used as an economic variable
span.quote: Our analysis of test scores uses five measures of cognitive skills (arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, mathematical knowledge, and coding speed) derived from the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB), which was administered to all sample participants in 1980 and 1981.

span.label: holding cognitive ability constant when comparing GED recipients with high school dropouts
span.note: eliminates: cognitive ability as the explanation of any wage difference attributed to the credential - and with it removed, the difference reverses rather than shrinking
span.quote: However, once cognitive ability is controlled for, GED recipients have the same or lower hourly wages as those of high school dropouts.

span.label: noncognitive skills
span.quote: This paper established that a low dimensional vector of cognitive and noncognitive skills explains a variety of labor market and behavioral outcomes.

span.label: cognitive skills
span.quote: Both cognitive and noncognitive skills are valued in the market.

span.label: normalizations
span.quote: As explained in Section (3.5) two normalizations are required to assure identification of the model. These set the scale of the factors.

span.label: measurement error
span.quote: Finally, there is the problem of measurement error. Test scores are imperfect proxies for latent cognitive and noncognitive abilities because they are affected by measured characteristics such as family background.

span.label: ASVAB
span.quote: Our analysis of test scores uses five measures of cognitive skills (arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, mathematical knowledge, and coding speed) derived from the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB), which was administered to all sample participants in 1980 and 1981.

span.label: Rotter Locus of Control Scale
span.quote: We use two attitudinal scales, the Rotter Locus of Control Scale and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, as our noncognitive measures. We choose these measures because of their availability in the NLSY.

span.label: coding speed
span.quote: We normalize the loadings (αCi (sT ), αNj (s(cid:48) T )) of the cognitive (f C) and noncognitive (f N ) factors to be equal to 1 in the equations associated with coding speed (ASVAB 5) and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale for individuals in grades 9 to 11 at the time of the test, respectively.

span.label: AFQT
span.quote: Neal and Johnson (1996) and Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004) demonstrate that each additional year of schooling increases an individual’s measured AFQT score by 2 to 4 percentage points, on average. This creates a reverse causality problem.

span.label: schooling
span.quote: Neal and Johnson (1996) and Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004) demonstrate that each additional year of schooling increases an individual’s measured AFQT score by 2 to 4 percentage points, on average. This creates a reverse causality problem.

span.label: ability → schooling
span.note: THE TWO CANNOT BE SEPARATED IN THIS STUDY - the DESIGN form (Q-286/Q-287). It bounds what the paper's own results can mean, and it lives in a methods paragraph where nothing downstream will find it. The confound is between the paper's own explanatory variables, so it bounds every coefficient in the table it is attached to.
span.quote: The least squares estimates reported in Table 1 cannot distinguish whether higher “ability” (as proxied by our cognitive measure) causes higher wages or whether additional years of schooling cause both higher measured cognitive scores and higher wages.

span.label: noncognitive skills - AS MEASURED: scores on attitude scales, which the paper calls at best imperfect measures of the individual's true ability
span.quote: In addition, scores on the attitude scales used to proxy noncognitive ability, as well as the cognitive scores, are likely to be affected by family background characteristics, and are at best imperfect measures of an individual’s true noncognitive and cognitive abilities.

span.label: noncognitive skills - AS MODELLED: a latent factor whose scale is fixed by normalization rather than by measurement
span.quote: As explained in Section (3.5) two normalizations are required to assure identification of the model. These set the scale of the factors.

span.label: Bayesian methods - used here for computation only, with the identification argument stated to be strictly classical and the priors asymptotically irrelevant
span.quote: Our use of Bayesian methods is only a computational convenience. Our identification analysis is strictly classical.17 Under our assumptions, the priors we use are asymptotically irrelevant.

span.label: test score - a quantity that depends on schooling completed AT THE TIME OF THE TEST, so the measurement is not independent of the outcome being explained
span.quote: In our model, the factor loadings in the test score equations depend on schooling at the time of the test. Therefore, for those who complete their schooling by the time of the test both latent factors affect both cognitive and noncognitive tests (albeit in an indirect way).

span.label: importance - IN THE SENSE THIS PAPER ADOPTS: the size of the skill gradient, how much an outcome moves when a person is moved across the distribution of one ability. ON THE RIVAL MEASURE THE RANKING REVERSES AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN THE SAME SENTENCE: cognitive skills 'explain much more of the variance of (log) wages', while by skill gradients the two are similar
span.quote: Although cognitive skills explain much more of the variance of (log) wages, their effects on (log) 33The standardized coefficient is obtained by multiplying the original coefficient by the standard deviation of the variable to which it is associated. 27 wages (as measured by skill gradients) are similar to the effects of the noncognitive traits.

span.label: importance - A THIRD SENSE THE PAPER NAMES AND EXPLICITLY DOES NOT CLAIM: equal strength in its own sense 'does not translate into equal cost of changing these skills', so the finding is silent on which ability is cheaper to change
span.quote: Of course, equal strength in the sense we have used it does not translate into equal cost of changing these skills.

span.label: contradicts → the "g" theory of Herrnstein and Murray (1994) and Jensen (1998)
span.quote: This evidence contradicts the “g” theory of human behavior espoused by Herrnstein and Murray (1994), Jensen (1998) and others that focuses on the primacy of cognitive skills in explaining socioeconomic outcomes.

span.label: builds-on → Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004)
span.quote: Building on the analysis of Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004), we correct measured test scores for these problems.

span.label: extends → the LISREL model of Jöreskog (1977) and the MIMIC model of Jöreskog and Goldberger (1975)
span.quote: Our method extends the LISREL model of J¨oreskog (1977) and the MIMIC model of J¨oreskog and Goldberger (1975) to account for the effects of choice variables (schooling) and background variables on the measurements of cognitive and noncognitive skills where the schooling, in turn, depends on the latent factors.

span.label: replicates → Neal and Johnson (1996); Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004); Heckman, Larenas, and Urzua (2004)
span.quote: The first finding corroborates the earlier analyses of Neal and Johnson (1996), Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004) and Heckman, Larenas, and Urzua (2004).

span.label: contradicts → Herrnstein and Murray (1994) and Herrnstein and Wilson (1985) on cognitive ability and crime
span.quote: Contrary to claims made by Herrnstein and Murray (1994) and Herrnstein and Wilson (1985), it is noncognitive ability that is the dominant factor in explaining different rates of participation in crime, and not cognitive ability.

span.label: contradicts → the single-skill signalling model of Arrow (1973) and Spence (1973)
span.quote: Our evidence that multiple abilities determine schooling challenges the conventional single skill signalling model due to Arrow (1973) and Spence (1973).

span.label: cognitive skills —operationalised-as→ ASVAB
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — Five subtests of a battery built to decide military eligibility - the paper says elsewhere that the AFQT composite 'is a general measure of trainability and a primary criterion of eligibility'. An instrument designed for a selection decision is here the measure of the construct.
span.quote: Our analysis of test scores uses five measures of cognitive skills (arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, mathematical knowledge, and coding speed) derived from the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB), which was administered to all sample participants in 1980 and 1981.

span.label: noncognitive skills —operationalised-as→ Rotter Locus of Control Scale
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE PAPER STATES ITS REASON FOR CHOOSING THEM AND IT IS NOT FITNESS: 'We choose these measures BECAUSE OF THEIR AVAILABILITY IN THE NLSY.' The construct carrying the paper's headline claim against Herrnstein and Murray is measured by a four-item abbreviated locus-of-control scale and a self-esteem scale, picked for what the survey happened to contain.
span.quote: We use two attitudinal scales, the Rotter Locus of Control Scale and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, as our noncognitive measures. We choose these measures because of their availability in the NLSY.

span.label: cognitive skills —operationalised-as→ coding speed
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE UNIT OF THE LATENT ABILITY IS SET BY WHICHEVER INDICATOR WAS GIVEN THE 1. The cognitive factor's loading is normalised to 1 on CODING SPEED (ASVAB 5) and the noncognitive factor's on the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, both 'for individuals in grades 9 to 11 at the time of the test' - so the scale is fixed by an indicator choice AND a schooling subgroup. The record already carries the existence of the normalisation; this names what the units are. NOTE THE HEADLINE COMPARISON DOES NOT DEPEND ON IT: the paper compares the two abilities by moving people between DECILES of each factor's own distribution, which is invariant to the scale.
span.quote: Our analysis of test scores uses five measures of cognitive skills (arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, mathematical knowledge, and coding speed) derived from the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB), which was administered to all sample participants in 1980 and 1981.

span.label: schooling —causes→ AFQT
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE PROXY IS CAUSED BY THE OUTCOME IT IS USED TO EXPLAIN: 'each additional year of schooling increases an individual's measured AFQT score by 2 TO 4 PERCENTAGE POINTS, on average. THIS CREATES A REVERSE CAUSALITY PROBLEM.' The paper says flatly in its conclusion, 'Schooling raises measured cognitive ability and measured noncognitive ability.' Naming this is the reason the paper builds a latent-factor model instead of regressing on test scores.
span.quote: Neal and Johnson (1996) and Hansen, Heckman, and Mullen (2004) demonstrate that each additional year of schooling increases an individual’s measured AFQT score by 2 to 4 percentage points, on average. This creates a reverse causality problem.

span.quote: This section of the paper presents a standard least squares analysis of the effects of cognitive

span.label: probit / multinomial discrete choice models
span.quote: These models are estimated using probit analysis and multinomial choice models.

span.label: Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation

span.quote: We use Bayesian MCMC methods to compute the sample likelihood.

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: The χ2 test for the null that schooling does not affect the means and factor loadings of the latent noncognitive test is 116.53 with 40 degrees of freedom.

span.label: A model with just two latent skills - one cognitive, one noncognitive - accounts for a wide range of labor-market and behavioral outcomes.
span.quote: This paper established that a low dimensional vector of cognitive and noncognitive skills explains a variety of labor market and behavioral outcomes.

span.label: Across many domains of social performance the two skill types matter about equally, contradicting the primacy-of-IQ view.
span.quote: For many dimensions of social performance cognitive and noncognitive skills are equally important.

span.label: Noncognitive skills shape schooling choices and additionally raise wages conditional on schooling.
span.quote: Noncognitive skills strongly influence schooling decisions, and also affect wages given schooling decisions.

span.label: Schooling itself raises measured test scores, so observed ability-wage relations are partly reverse causation.
span.quote: Schooling raises measured test scores.

span.label: Once corrected for schooling and family background, male GED holders look worse than ordinary dropouts on noncognitive ability although they are better on cognitive ability.
span.quote: Male GEDs have a worse noncognitive ability distribution than dropouts.

span.label: Noncognitive rather than cognitive ability is what mainly explains differences in criminal participation.
span.quote: the dominant factor in explaining different rates of participation in crime, and not cognitive ability.

span.label: The two latent skills carry different hedonic prices in the labor markets of different schooling levels.
span.quote: The skills are priced differently in different schooling markets.

span.label: Estimated returns to ability shrink when test scores are corrected for the schooling attained at test date, showing that endogenous test scores bias conventional OLS estimates upward.
